It clearly shows that the ʿiṣam obtained by Banū ʿAbd Manāf from governments in and around the Hijaz took the form of treaties. The figurative meaning of the word ʿiṣam itself supports this, since it can mean a covenant or pledge.

The same explanation, and the fact that historians generally accept it, also shows how far the Quraysh aristocracy—represented by Banū ʿAbd Manāf—had come to dominate trade in western Arabia during the second half of the fifth century CE.

Hāshim’s assumption of responsibility for providing water and food to pilgrims is associated with the year 464 CE. By then, Banū ʿAbd Manāf had enough power to conclude treaties and organize the region’s relations with foreign powers at the level of kings and rulers, according to what best served their commercial interests and social privileges.

Pre-Islamic poetry also gives us evidence for two points. First, it supports the interpretation of ʿiṣam as a covenant or treaty. Second, it confirms the economic and social dominance of Banū ʿAbd Manāf within Quraysh and Meccan society.
One example is the following poem by Maṭrūd ibn Kaʿb al-Khuzāʿī:
O man who is moving on with all his baggage, why did you not stay with the house of ʿAbd Manāf?
May your mother lose you! Had you stayed with them, they would have protected you from hunger and hardship.
They are the ones who secure covenants from distant lands, and who set out on the journeys of the īlāf.
Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥanash al-Sulamī, Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf’s maternal brother, says:
My brother Hāshim is no ordinary brother. By God, Hāshim is neither lacking nor idle.
Goodness is wrapped around him, and the grave-digger digs for him; he secures the pact and travels on behalf of those who stay behind.

The advanced way in which the Meccan aristocracy organized its commercial relations with the outside world had major economic and social effects on the lives of the people of the Hijaz, in both towns and desert communities.
First, it created stable arrangements for these commercial relations instead of leaving them to chance or to shifts in political conditions.
Second, it opened wide new areas for imports, exports, and the role of Arab traders as middlemen between eastern and western trade.

Third, it was a major factor in spreading the use of money throughout tribal society. Meccan merchants dealt in the different currencies used in the foreign countries with which they traded. As we said earlier, this brought into tribal society one of the most important forces speeding up its breakdown and dissolution.

Fourth, it drew large numbers of people from both towns and the desert into commercial activity. Some helped finance caravans at different levels. Many others worked as caravan guides or guards, or provided essential services at stopping points along overland routes and at seaports. Others traded consumer goods with the caravans and developed small-scale trade between tribes.

Tribal chiefs also received tolls, taxes, and valuable gifts in exchange for protecting caravans. They then invested their earnings in large commercial ventures. This widened the economic and social gap between the chiefs and ordinary members of their tribes, and made social inequality an increasingly powerful force in breaking down the tribal system.

The economic and social changes described above made another development necessary. They created the material basis for a form of political organization suited to those changes—an organization capable of containing them and protecting the gains they had produced.
That material basis was private ownership of the means of production, together with the use of money to exploit others by controlling the labour of people who owned no property.

As we saw earlier in our discussion of pre-Islamic society, this basis appeared in several forms: ownership of slaves as a means of production, ownership of agricultural land, and ownership of money invested in trade and in lending at interest.

We also saw that economic development on this basis had already begun to break down the structure of the old tribal system. It created inequalities among members of society in living standards, in the distribution of wealth and products, and also in individual rights and social position—even among members of the same tribe or clan. In doing so, it began to move beyond the traditional rules of tribal life.

Put another way, pre-Islamic society was beginning to divide into groups whose economic interests came into conflict with those of other groups. In other words, it was moving toward the beginnings of class division.

These economic and social inequalities had already begun to produce early forms of social breakdown and rebellion, visible in groups such as the outlaws and expelled men. This was a sign that inequality was beginning to turn into genuine social conflict, laying the foundation for a division of society into classes, even if that division was still only at an early stage.
It was natural for the first signs of this process to appear in Mecca before they appeared in the desert.

Before this change, Quraysh had not been fundamentally different from the people of the desert in the structure of their tribal life. They were a clan like other Arab clans of the pre-Islamic period. Kinship and descent governed both their internal relations and their relations with other clans and tribes.

But the economic forces we discussed earlier developed in Mecca’s commercial society before they developed in the desert. It was therefore natural that the old Bedouin system of tribal relations should begin to break down in Mecca first.

The breakdown of that system in Mecca also helped prepare the conditions for its later breakdown in the desert. This followed from Mecca’s commercial, economic, and religious importance, not only in western Arabia but throughout the peninsula, and from the influence that this position gave it over tribal relations across the region.
This influence was closely tied to the control exercised by the Quraysh leadership over economic activity in many parts of the peninsula.
As the old system of primitive communal relations broke down, some new form of social relationship had to take its place.

We have already seen the main economic and social foundations of this new form. Commercial and financial wealth was becoming concentrated in the hands of a section of Quraysh in Mecca and of tribal chiefs in the desert. The same was true of ownership of the means of production: slaves, livestock, rights to use irrigation water and grazing land, and the richest productive land around Ṭāʾif.

The economic dominance of the Quraysh aristocracy therefore had to produce its own “political” institution. Such an institution was needed to organize the relationship of power between this ruling group and the other social groups it exploited economically. It also had to give that relationship a legal form suited to the historical conditions of the time, and to impose its “legitimacy” on those same groups. They were now expected to submit politically to the “ruling” Quraysh aristocracy just as they already submitted to it economically.
The Meccan malaʾ, or council of notables, was the first expression of Quraysh dominance in a form that we could describe, in modern language, as “political.”
At that stage, the malaʾ represented the earliest embryo of a state: the political institution of the class that dominates economic activity in a class society.
At the same time, it represented the birth of that class itself within pre-Islamic society.
Historically, the Meccan malaʾ was made up of the city’s leading merchants, moneylenders, and slave owners. It concentrated all forms of authority in a single body—the malaʾ itself.

This body strengthened its authority with a force of repression, as reports about the Aḥābīsh of Mecca suggest. From these reports, we understand that the malaʾ used the Aḥābīsh as armed police. They guarded the Kaaba and also the homes of members of the malaʾ.
This use of guards is important for our argument.

Establishing armed guards around the Kaaba did not simply mean protecting its religious sanctity. It also meant protecting the wealth of Quraysh, who had taken advantage of that sanctity by using the Kaaba as a place to store their money.
Likewise, guards posted around their homes were meant to protect them from “the anger of the discontented groups in the city of Mecca and the resentment of poor pilgrims.”

The rise of the malaʾ as a form of “political” authority representing the group that controlled wealth and exploited others appears to have been historically connected with the rise of the Quraysh commercial aristocracy.
We have no sources or documents showing that a body with this economic and social character existed before the Quraysh aristocracy took control of Mecca and assumed responsibility for the Kaaba.

Everything we know about the leadership of Mecca and the custodianship of the Kaaba before Quraysh suggests that these roles were limited to supervising the pilgrimage and leading pilgrims as they performed the pre-Islamic rituals during the pilgrimage season.

Leadership rested on a purely tribal basis. A tribe or clan might gain precedence because it possessed some form of tribal honour recognized by pre-Islamic custom, or because it had defeated another group in intertribal warfare.

The traditional accounts of Mecca before Islam tell us that the custodianship of the Kaaba and the leadership of Mecca passed successively through the South Arabian tribe of Jurhum, then the tribes of Quḍāʿa, and finally Quraysh.

Jurhum established itself in Mecca by the second method—that is, through military victory. Even during the period of Khuzāʿa, Jurhum retained some part in the administration of pilgrimage. A group called Ṣūfa, belonging to Jurhum, had the authority to give pilgrims permission to leave ʿArafāt for Minā and to begin the stoning of the pillars.
This lasted until the rule of Khuzāʿa ended and control of Mecca passed fully to Quraysh.
Before the rise of Quraysh, then, the custodianship of the Kaaba and the leadership of Mecca rested on traditional tribal foundations.
But things changed greatly when Quraysh came to power.

It is true that the traditional accounts describe fighting between Quṣayy, his people, and his allies on one side, and first the Jurhumite elite and then Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr on the other. In that sense, Quraysh under Quṣayy reached power by the same route as those before them: through fighting.
But the important question is not the fighting itself.
What matters is Quṣayy’s claim that he had a greater right to rule, and the way the traditional historians explain that claim.

The Arabic sources usually rely on Ibn al-Kalbī when telling the story of this historical change, while some use the account of Ibn Isḥāq. There is no real contradiction between the two versions. They differ mainly in one respect.
The first explains the basis on which Quṣayy claimed a greater right to control the Kaaba and rule Mecca. The second concentrates more on the details of the story and its outcome.
If we put the explanation together with the outcome, along with the details common to both accounts, the real meaning of this historical change becomes much clearer.
We have already referred to the explanation. The reports say of Quṣayy:

“…when Ḥulayl ibn Ḥubshiyya of Khuzāʿa died, and Quṣayy’s children had become numerous, his wealth had grown, and his honour had become great, he saw that he had a greater right to the House and to the affairs of Mecca…”
The wording suggests that Quṣayy’s claim rested above all on the fact that he had become wealthy.

Having many children by itself was not enough to establish such a right. And the “great honour” mentioned in the report appears to have been something he acquired at a particular point in his life. The wording makes this clear. It was therefore not the inherited honour that had traditionally counted in tribal society. It was a new kind of honour gained through Quṣayy’s success in acquiring money and wealth.
The accounts of what Quṣayy did in old age support this interpretation.
They say that he transferred his authority to his eldest son, ʿAbd al-Dār:

“When Quṣayy became old and weak, ʿAbd al-Dār was his eldest son (888), while ʿAbd Manāf had gained greater honour during his brother’s lifetime (…) Quṣayy said to ʿAbd al-Dār: ‘By God, I will raise you to the level of the others, even though they have gained more honour than you…’”
These texts make it clear that “honour” here means success in acquiring wealth.
As for the outcome, which interests Ibn Isḥāq more than the explanation, his account says after giving the details:

“…Quṣayy took charge of the House and the affairs of Mecca. He gathered his people from their settlements and brought them into Mecca. He became ruler over his people, the inhabitants of Mecca, and they accepted his rule. Quṣayy was therefore the first descendant of Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy to gain a kingship that his people obeyed. He held responsibility for the custodianship of the Kaaba, the provision of water and food to pilgrims, the assembly, and the war banner. In this way he gained all the honours of Mecca. He divided Mecca into quarters among his people and settled each group of Quraysh in the part of the city that later remained associated with them.”
From all this, we can see that the transfer of Meccan leadership to Quraysh did not rest on an established tribal custom, nor was military victory the main principle used to justify it.
Its real basis was something new.

Economic and social development had given wealth a new kind of power. Money had begun to shape the logic of events, change the standards by which people were judged, and influence the direction of the new social reality that was taking form.

The earlier reports also describe a judgment issued by a man chosen to arbitrate between Quṣayy’s side and the opposing side of Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr, after heavy fighting had finally led them to seek peace.
The reports say that Yaʿmur ibn ʿAwf ibn Kaʿb gave the following judgment:

“Quṣayy has a greater right to the Kaaba and the affairs of Mecca than Khuzāʿa. Any blood shed by Quṣayy among Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr is cancelled, and he may cast it beneath his feet. But for any blood shed by Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr among Quraysh and Banū Kināna, the blood-money must be paid. And the way must be cleared for Quṣayy ibn Kilāb to take control of the Kaaba and Mecca.”
“From that day Yaʿmur ibn ʿAwf was called al-Sharrākh because of the blood claims he laid out and waived.”
This is certainly a strange judgment. It immediately attracts attention.
But it also tells us that the new factor that objectively gave Quṣayy priority over those who had ruled the Kaaba and Mecca before him was also behind the striking form of Yaʿmur ibn ʿAwf’s decision.
Why did Quṣayy have a greater right to the Kaaba and the government of Mecca than Khuzāʿa?

Why was the blood Quṣayy had shed among Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr simply cancelled, with no punishment and no blood-money, while Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr were required to pay compensation for the blood they had shed among Quraysh and Kināna?

If such a harsh judgment had fitted comfortably within the tribal customs and traditions of pre-Islamic Arabia, it would not have attracted enough attention for people to give its author the name al-Sharrākh because of the blood claims his decision had swept aside and placed “beneath the feet” of Quṣayy without any apparent justification.
Does that mean the ruling was completely arbitrary?
Its outward form may look arbitrary, but its underlying content had a real historical logic that “justified” it.
The same economic development that gave Quṣayy “all the honour of Mecca” also provided the real historical logic behind a judgment of this kind.
And it was this same new logic that all the opposing sides accepted when they submitted to the judgment of al-Sharrākh without protest.
The Nadwa, or Assembly, and the malaʾ gave this same historical reality a concrete human and organizational form.

The Nadwa was the meeting place of the malaʾ in Quṣayy’s house. It served the newly born “class” created by the breakdown of the old primitive tribal order, and it served the embryonic “institution” emerging from the same conditions. The new class needed a new system of its own, and that system needed authority and institutions suited to its historical position.
The traditional historians have given us more than enough information about this Nadwa to form a clear picture of it.

“Built the Assembly House and placed its door facing the House—that is, the Kaaba. All the affairs of Quraysh were conducted there: anything concerning marriage contracts, war, or consultation among themselves. Even when a girl reached the age when she began wearing a full garment, that garment was first cut for her there, and she was then taken back to her family.

“No war banner for Quraysh, or for any people allied with them, was raised anywhere except in the Assembly House. No boy was circumcised except there. No Quraysh caravan departed without setting out from there, and when they returned they stopped there first. (…) It was called the Nadwa because Quraysh used to gather there, for matters good and bad alike.”
This account appears, with only small differences in wording, throughout the traditional sources.
As a representative example of the others, it shows that the Meccan malaʾ turned the Nadwa into a broad and almost absolute authority.
Even the private affairs of Mecca’s inhabitants came under its supervision, along with public affairs in both peace and war.
It dealt especially with contracts, transactions, and everything connected with economic and social life, as well as the affairs of religious festivals and pilgrimage seasons.

The Nadwa, acting in the name of the malaʾ, therefore exercised powers resembling legislative, executive, judicial, and administrative authority, all concentrated in a single body: the malaʾ, the upper stratum of Quraysh, or in other words the commercial aristocracy of Mecca.
As another sign that authority was restricted to this privileged group, the malaʾ limited admission to the Assembly House to members of Quraysh who had reached the age of forty.
The descendants of Quṣayy were the exception. All of them were allowed to enter, even before the age of forty. This was a privilege of those who held power.

The traditional historians also say that when Quṣayy became old, he transferred responsibility for the Nadwa, the custodianship of the Kaaba, the provision of water and food to pilgrims, and the war banner to his eldest son ʿAbd al-Dār. This is the version given in al-Balādhurī’s Ansāb and Ibn Saʿd’s Ṭabaqāt.
Al-Yaʿqūbī says that Quṣayy gave him the Nadwa alone, while al-Azraqī says that he gave him the Nadwa, the custodianship of the Kaaba, and the war banner.
The accounts differ in detail, but all agree that the Nadwa was given to ʿAbd al-Dār.
What can we learn from this?
